Dataflow & Tiling Strategies in Edge-AI FPGA

Accelerators: A Comprehensive Literature Review

Zhaoqin Li Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science

Samueli School of Engineering University of California, Irvine

Irvine, CA, USA Email: zhaoqil3@uci.edu

Edge-AI applications demand high-throughput, low-latency inference on FPGAs under tight resource and power constraints. This survey provides a comprehensive review of two key architectural decisions for FPGAbased neural network accelerators: (i) the dataflow (the order and manner in which data is moved and reused on chip), and (ii) the tiling/blocking strategy (how large tensors are partitioned to fit on-chip). We first present a broadened taxonomy of canonical dataflow styles—Weight-Stationary, Output-Stationary, Row-Stationary, and No-Local-Reuse—including formal definitions, pseudo-code/diagrams, and real FPGA examples. We then discuss analytical frameworks (MAESTRO, Timeloop) and compare them with a concise feature table, illustrating how they model reuse, performance, and hardware costs, and include a case study of a 3×3 convolution layer to demonstrate typical tool outputs. Next, we detail multi-level tiling and loop unrolling/pipelining strategies for FPGAs, clarifying how each memory tier (registers, LUTRAM, BRAM, HBM) can be exploited. Our four case studies—FINN, FINN- R, FlightLLM, and SSR—highlight distinct dataflows (from binary streaming to hybrid sparse transformations) and tiling patterns. We include a unified comparison matrix covering platform, precision, throughput, resource utilization, and energy efficiency, plus small block diagrams for each design. We conclude by examining design automation trade-offs among HLS, DSL, and hand-coded RTL, offering a “lessons learned” summary box, and charting future research directions in partial reconfiguration, hybrid dataflows, and domain-specific compiler flows for next-generation edge AI FPGA accelerators.

Index Terms

FPGA, Edge AI, Dataflow, Tiling, DNN Accelerator, MAESTRO, Timeloop, FINN, SSR, FlightLLM

I. INTRODUCTION Deploying deep neural networks (DNNs) at the edge devices demands high performance per watt under limited on-chip memory and power budgets. FPGAs excel here by enabling customized parallelism, bitwidths, and memory hierarchies, achieving energy-efficient throughput compared to CPUs or GPUs [1], [2]. However, realizing these benefits requires (1) careful dataflow selection to maximize on-chip reuse of weights and activations, and (2) optimal tiling/blocking to match data shapes to limited BRAM/URAM/HBM.

In this paper, we: 1) Present an expanded taxonomy of four canonical dataflow styles for DNN accelerators on FPGAs (Section II). 2) Compare analytical frameworks (MAESTRO vs. Timeloop) for data-centric modeling (Section III). 3) Examine tiling, loop unrolling, pipelining, and multi-level buffering in detail (Section IV). 4) Survey four case studies—FINN, FINN-R, FlightLLM, SSR—with a unified quantitative comparison (Section V).

5) Assess design automation approaches (HLS vs. DSL vs. RTL) and highlight key productivity tradeoffs (Section VI). 6) Conclude with Future Directions and a succinct Conclusion (Sections VII–VIII). Readers seeking broad background on DNN architectures are referred to [7]. Our focus is on edge-tier FPGA designs, from binarized CNNs to large language models.

II. DATAFLOW TAXONOMY Dataflow defines how the nested loops of a DNN layer (over input channels, output channels, spatial axes) are mapped onto hardware PEs and on-chip memory [5]. We present four canonical styles below, each with a short pseudo-code or snippet, a small block diagram, and an example FPGA design.

A. Weight-Stationary (WS)

Definition: In Weight-Stationary dataflow, each PE keeps its filter weights locally, and partial sums / activations stream through. Once weights are loaded, they remain ‘stationary‘ on-chip as inputs are cycled across them.

Algorithm 1 Weight-Stationary Dataflow

1: for all tiles of input activations do

Load tile into local buffer

for all PE in array do

partial sum ←0

for all elements in tile do

partial sum ←partial sum + weight[PE] × activation[element]

output[PE] ←partial sum
Fig. 1. Weight-Stationary dataflow

Example FPGA Accelerator: Many systolic-array-like designs use WS. For instance, Google’s TPU v1 had a weight-stationary strategy in its 2D systolic array (though it is an ASIC). On FPGAs, some matrix-multiply IP cores or HLS-based designs pin weights in BRAM to minimize re-fetching [1].

B. Output-Stationary (OS)

Definition: In Output-Stationary, partial sums for a specific output element (or a small group of output channels) remain in local PE registers or buffers until all input channels are processed, after which the final result is written back to memory.

Example FPGA Accelerator: Some earlier FPGA CNN pipelines used OS by accumulating the result of one output pixel in local registers. ShiDianNao (an ASIC) also exemplifies OS, streaming input data across PEs that keep partial sums in place. Eyeriss (v1) effectively uses an OS-like scheme for many conv layers [7].

Algorithm 2 Output Stationary GEMV-like Dataflow

1: for out ch ←0 to Out do

partial sum[out ch] ←0

4: for in ch ←0 to In do

for out ch ←0 to Out do

partial sum[out ch] ←partial sum[out ch] + weight[out ch, in ch] × input[in ch]

9: Write partial sum[] to memory
Fig. 2. Output-Stationary dataflow

C. Row-Stationary (RS)

Definition: Proposed in Eyeriss [7], Row-Stationary keeps a strip (or row) of activations and partial sums on each PE, so that all relevant filters can be reused across them. It balances weight and activation reuse.

Algorithm 3 Row-wise Tiled Convolution with PE-Level Accumulation

1: for all rows r in output do

Load row r of input tile into row buffer

for all filter sets do

for all processing elements (PEs) in row r do

partial sum[PE] ←partial sum[PE] + MAC(row buffer[PE], filter chunk)

. . . (e.g., update filter chunk or control)

Store completed row r to output memory
Fig. 3. Row-Stationary dataflow

Example FPGA Accelerator: Eyeriss was first demonstrated as an ASIC. On FPGAs, row-stationary is less common but still relevant where the cost of local reuse for both weights and partial sums is balanced. Some HLS-based designs adapt RS to minimize DRAM access by storing partial sums row-by-row in BRAM.

D. No-Local-Reuse (NLR)

Definition: Also called “global-buffer reuse.” PEs have minimal local storage; data (weights, activations, partial sums) is read from a large shared buffer (or high-bandwidth memory) each time. This simplifies control but increases buffer bandwidth demand.

Algorithm 4 Element-wise Output Dataflow with Global Buffer Access

1: for all elements e in output do

partial sum ←0

for in ch ←0 to I do

partial sum ←partial sum + global buffer.read(in ch) × global buffer.read(weight idx)

global buffer.write(output idx, partial sum)
Fig. 4. No-Local-Reuse Dataflow

Example FPGA Accelerator: DianNao (ASIC) used a large eDRAM “global buffer,” with minimal caching in the PEs. On FPGAs, some streaming matrix-multiply cores adopt a “flat read” from HBM + immediate compute + write-back.

III. ANALYTICAL FRAMEWORKS FOR DATAFLOW & REUSE Two widely used analytical frameworks for modeling DNN dataflow on custom accelerators are MAE- STRO [6] and Timeloop [8]. Both tools systematically explore loop order, tiling factors, and data reuse patterns to estimate cycle count, energy consumption, and on-chip buffer usage.

a) Comparison.: b) Case Study: 3×3 Convolution Layer Analysis.: To illustrate typical results, we analyze a 3 × 3 convolution from ResNet-50 [9] (64 input →64 output channels on 56 × 56 feature maps, batch 1) on a hypothetical 256-PE accelerator with a two-level memory (256 kB global buffer, 1 kB PE-local buffer) using a weight-stationary dataflow.

• Weight reuse: ≈3,136× (each 3×3 filter remains local and is applied across all spatial positions) [6].

• Activation reuse: up to 576× via spatial broadcast and temporal accumulation [6].

• Off-chip traffic: ∼0.87 MB (weights + activations) versus 440 MB if no on-chip reuse [6].

• Latency: ≈5 × 105 cycles (ideal double buffering, full PE utilization) [6].

• Energy breakdown: dominated by on-chip MAC and SRAM accesses; DRAM accounts for ≪5% of total energy [6]. Timeloop (with Accelergy) yields comparable metrics:

• Cycle count: ≈4.5 ×105 cycles [8].

• Energy profile: ∼2% DRAM energy, remainder in PEs and on-chip buffers [8].

• Mapping exploration: identifies weight-stationary as energy-optimal, with energy variance up to 11× across alternative tilings [11]. This case study demonstrates how both frameworks expose data reuse, bandwidth requirements, and performance/energy trade-offs prior to any HLS or RTL implementation, guiding accelerator designers toward near-optimal dataflow strategies and avoiding costly rework.

IV. TILING & BLOCKING STRATEGIES IN FPGA DESIGN Efficient tiling and loop transformations are central to implementing dataflows on FPGAs with limited on-chip memory. This section dissects: (1) Two-Level Tiling, (2) Loop Unrolling & Pipelining, (3) Buffer Hierarchies & Double Buffering, and (4) Multi-Level Tiling for deeper memory tiers.

A. Two-Level Tiling

Definition and Rationale: Large DNN layers typically exceed on-chip capacity, so we block data into outer tiles (resident in DRAM/HBM) and inner tiles (resident in BRAM/LUTRAM). Each inner tile is processed fully before fetching the next, reducing external memory accesses [2].

• Outer tile size is chosen so that a large chunk can be loaded into on-chip buffers once and reused many times.

• Inner tile size is tuned to the PE-array shape (e.g., 16 × 16) so that the data can be consumed in a single pipeline. Guidelines for Choosing Tile Sizes:

• Fit in BRAM: The tile must not exceed available BRAM or URAM capacity.

• Utilize DSPs fully: Align tile dimension with the number of parallel multipliers to minimize underflow.

• Amortize loading cost: A tile that is too small may incur overhead from repeated DRAM transfers.

B. Loop Unrolling & Pipelining

Unrolling: By duplicating hardware for inner-loop iterations, throughput increases linearly with the unroll factor, constrained by LUT/DSP availability.

Algorithm 5 Loop Unrolling with Factor 16

1: #pragma HLS UNROLL factor=16

2: for i ←0 to tile size exclusive do

Perform parallel operations on 16 elements

Pipelining: Achieving Initiation Interval (II) = 1 means each loop iteration can start every cycle, overlapping compute.

Expected II Improvements:

resolving deps IIoptimized = 1

Careful memory partitioning and accumulation logic (e.g., tree reductions) help reach II = 1.

C. Buffer Hierarchies & Double Buffering

Modern FPGAs offer multiple on-chip tiers: 1) Registers / LUTRAM: Minimal capacity, but single-cycle access. 2) BRAM: Larger capacity (tens to hundreds of kbits) with 1–2 read ports. 3) UltraRAM: Embedded blocks with deeper capacity (on some devices). 4) HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory): On-package DRAM with ∼300+ GB/s. Double Buffering is crucial: for tile n, while it is being processed by the PE array, tile n+1 is fetched from external memory into a spare buffer. This overlap hides memory latency.

Algorithm 6 Double Buffering Flow

1: while true do

Load tile n + 1 into buffer B

Compute tile n from buffer A

Swap(buffer A, buffer B)

5: end while

D. Multi-Level Tiling

Beyond two levels, one can exploit a deeper hierarchy: e.g., outer tiles in HBM, mid-level tiles in BRAM, and inner sub-tiles in registers or LUTRAM. This is increasingly relevant on devices like Xilinx Versal or Alveo U280, which combine HBM, URAM, and distributed RAM. Typically:

• The outermost tile is sized to the HBM capacity and bandwidth.

• Intermediate tiles are staged in URAM/BRAM for partial reuse.

• The innermost sub-tile is streamed through the PE pipeline with minimal buffering in LUTRAM/registers. By carefully partitioning data at each level, accelerators can minimize off-chip traffic and keep the PE array continuously busy.

V. CASE STUDIES OF EDGE-AI FPGA ACCELERATORS To illustrate how different dataflows and tiling strategies combine in real designs, we review four exemplary accelerators: (1) FINN, (2) FINN-R, (3) FlightLLM, (4) SSR. Table II then unifies their key metrics (platform, precision, throughput, resource usage, energy efficiency). Small block diagrams highlight each design’s data movement.

A. FINN: BNN Streaming

Proposed by Umuroglu et al. [1], FINN accelerates binarized convolutional networks. Each layer is mapped as a streaming pipeline with weight-stationary dataflow (the 1-bit weights stay in LUT arrays), while 1-bit activations flow through in a sliding-window manner. Intermediate layer outputs are kept on-chip in shift registers or small BRAM.

Input

Sliding Window −−−−−−−−→XNOR+POPCOUNT

Bitwise Accum −−−−−−−→Output

Due to full pipeline parallelization and minimal bitwidth, FINN achieves high frame rates (10k+ fps on CIFAR-10) on modest FPGAs.

B. FINN-R: Automated QNN Framework

FINN-R [2] generalizes FINN to 2–8 bit quantized networks and provides an automated toolflow. Designers specify throughput/resource goals, and FINN-R’s cost model chooses unroll factors, tiling parameters, and layer pipelines. Dataflow remains streaming with partial weight-stationary blocks. Example usage:

C. FlightLLM: Sparse DSP for Large Language Models

FlightLLM [3] targets Transformers on Alveo U280 with HBM plus configurable “sparse DSP” chains. Weights are partially pruned; dense blocks are loaded from HBM, but zeros are skipped. The dataflow is partially output-stationary for each token’s vector, combined with weight-streaming from HBM.

D. SSR: Spatial-Sequential Hybrid on Versal

SSR [4] exploits multi-engine parallelism on Xilinx Versal ACAP. It partitions Transformer layers across multiple accelerators, each using a mixture of on-chip AIEs for matrix multiply and PL for layernorm or activation. Dataflow is row-stationary within each AIE cluster, with cross-layer partial sums passed in on-chip buffers.

VI. DESIGN AUTOMATION APPROACHES Accelerating DNNs on FPGAs can be done via HLS, domain-specific languages (DSL), or hand-coded RTL. Table III contrasts these approaches, focusing on code size, compile times, typical resource overhead, and productivity gains.
TABLE III HLS VS. DSL VS. RTL: SIDE-BY-SIDE COMPARISON

HLS DSL RTL (HDL)

LoC (approx.) Medium Very low High Compile Time Hours Hours–days Days–weeks Productivity Medium High Low Overhead (LUT/DSP) +10–30% +20–40% Baseline

Lessons Learned (Callout Box):

• Automation Gains: HLS/DSL can reduce design time ≈5× vs. RTL, at a cost of ∼30% more LUT usage.

• Parallelism Leverage: Automated flows still let you specify unroll factors; not purely “pushbutton.”

• Verification Ease: DSL-level simulation is faster; verifying each cycle in RTL is time-consuming.

• Future Trend: Hybrid approaches combining DSL for coarse architecture with selective handtuned kernels.

• Hybrid Dataflow Mappings: Future accelerators may dynamically switch between weight-stationary and output-stationary (or row-stationary) depending on layer geometry and sparsity.

• Partial Reconfiguration: FPGAs can reconfigure part of the fabric to tailor each layer’s dataflow or tiling. Overheads must be balanced with potential gains.

• Domain-Specific Compilers: Building on MAESTRO/Timeloop, next-gen DSLs could unify code generation, loop transformations, and memory mapping for diverse networks (CNN, LSTM, Transformer) with minimal user intervention.

VIII. CONCLUSION We presented a comprehensive overview of dataflow styles and tiling strategies for FPGA-based DNN accelerators. By dissecting canonical patterns—Weight-Stationary, Output-Stationary, Row-Stationary, No- Local-Reuse—and comparing frameworks like MAESTRO vs. Timeloop, we illustrated how to systematically exploit on-chip reuse. Our deep dive into tiling (two-level and multi-level) and loop transformations

underscores the complexity in balancing memory capacity, bandwidth, and DSP usage. Four case studies (FINN, FINN-R, FlightLLM, SSR) reveal success in tackling different model sizes and workload constraints, highlighting design automation’s growing importance. Looking ahead, partial reconfiguration, hybrid dataflows, and more sophisticated compilers promise to further shrink the gap between flexible FPGA solutions and the aggressive performance demands of edge AI.
